title: What Nobody Sees
text: 1 What Nobody Sees I spent five years as a laboratory specialist inside a provincial CDC in Vietnam. I am writing this proposal now because I lived through these events myself. I do not write as an academic who studied these systems from a distance. I write from the physical memory of my own hands. To understand the proposal I am presenting, we must look closely at how the samples arrived in the second half of 2021. The arrival of these specimens was the first critical step of our daily labor. The samples were collected in the field by health workers. Sometimes, I went out into the field to collect these samples myself. Other times, the district health centers gathered the specimens and sent them back to our central provincial facility. Every single batch of these samples arrived at our laboratory inside cold boxes. We did not have specialized or uniform medical transport equipment. Instead, we had to rely on whatever cold boxes were available to the units at that moment. These cold boxes were transported to us by whatever means possible. Some came in an ambulance if the unit was fortunate enough to have one. If an ambulance was not available, the units carried the boxes in any vehicle they could find. The specimens travelled in standard triple packaging: tubes of transport medium inside sealed bags, inside larger bags, inside the cold box. This specific packaging protocol was passed down through a very clear chain of training. The Pasteur Institute first taught the protocol to the provincial CDC. The CDC then passed this training down to the frontline workers. From there, the frontline workers showed each other how to perform the collection and the packing. The samples we received came from many different sources. Some were collected from quarantine facilities housing citizens who had returned from abroad. Others came from deep inside the local prisons. Some samples even came from the dead. Each of these different sources sent their specimens to our laboratory in the same types of packages. Eventually, the sheer quantity of these incoming shipments became too much for our testing facility to hold. When the rising sample volume completely overwhelmed our laboratory space, we had no choice but to move the containers. The incoming cold boxes had to go out into the wide corridor. They lined the hallway in long rows. This physical arrival of cold boxes, nested bags, and container tubes was our daily reality. By looking at how these samples arrived, we see the foundation of our work and the heavy responsibility of maintaining the trace. This is the background for the system I propose today. The dangerous part of a pandemic is easy to picture: protective suits, negative pressure, live virus. That part was real. It was not where we lost the most. The deepest bottleneck of the entire pandemic did not occur in a high-security bio-isolation unit. It was a simple desk task. It happened in an ordinary administrative office. Labelling sounds like fieldwork, something done in the heat of the moment under layers of gear. The truth is much more mundane. We did the labelling before anyone ever went out to collect a single sample. We sat at wooden desks. We wore our everyday, ordinary clothes. No protective gowns were needed because there were no active samples in the room yet. The virus was not present. There was only a stack of blank sheets, a printer, and thousands of empty, clean container tubes. These tubes contained only the transport medium. The medium was a sterile, red liquid waiting for a swab. Before those tubes could be sent out to hospitals, clinics, or quarantine camps, they had to be marked. Each tube needed a specific identity. So we sat there in our civilian clothes, matching lists on a computer screen to physical labels. We stuck the printed paper onto the cold plastic of the empty tubes. It was silent, repetitive work. It was administrative. Yet, if a single mistake was made during this quiet desk task, the entire scientific apparatus downstream fell apart. A typo in a birth year or a misaligned barcode on an empty tube meant a real person would lose their connection to their test. They would wait at home for a result that could never be traced back to them. The danger of a broken trace did not start with a sneeze or a cough. It started with a pen or a keyboard in a quiet office. The dramatic work in full protective suits is what makes the news. But the real bottleneck, the place where the system actually choked, was a simple desk job. It was a matter of administrative organization. We were fighting a war of logistics with the tools of an office clerk. By understanding that our greatest barrier was a paperwork bottleneck, we can see the true value of the solution I am proposing. Containment infrastructure does its own job and nothing here replaces it. This is a different gap, upstream of the bench, and a much cheaper one. Fix the trace where it begins: secure the information on the desk before the tube ever meets the patient. Today, as I write down this proposal, I want to describe the exact workflow we built because it holds the core of my entire idea. Our daily work always began with a list of patient names. This collection list did not arrive in a formal or highly structured digital format. It usually came to us through a simple email or a common messaging app. We would open the message and print the raw list onto sheets of paper. Then the slow, manual work began. I sat at my wooden desk and converted that printed paper list by hand into a digital Excel file. This was not a sophisticated program. It was just an ordinary spreadsheet, but we used it as our central database to organize the chaos. We linked this Excel database directly to a barcode printer. That link was the whole of it. Through it, we assigned each patient a unique identification number. This unique ID did something very important. It tied the physical sample directly to the living person from the very start. This connection remained solid throughout the entire lifecycle of the test. The ID bound the person to the sample from the moment of collection in the field. It stayed with the tube during processing inside our laboratory. It guided the data all the way through to the final returned result. This was before the peak. We were doing wide screening, and the constraint was not the bench. It was the desk. Every patient’s details were copied out by hand, and that copying set the ceiling for the whole laboratory. We could move fewer than three hundred samples a day, and no part of that limit had anything to do with virology. Once the spreadsheet drove the barcode printer, each person carried a unique identifier and each tube carried it too. The identity was fixed at the desk, before anyone went to the field. That one change lifted us to roughly four thousand samples a day. I want to be exact about why, because the obvious reading is wrong. A label printer does not make a thermocycler faster. What it did was separate identity from analysis. With identifiers already assigned, we could pool samples into a single reaction and the record still held the list of who was in that pool, without anyone writing names on a worksheet. If a pool came back positive we broke it apart and ran the members individually, and nothing had to be typed in again. When positivity was low we pooled more. When it rose we pooled less, or ran singles. The testing strategy could change in a morning and the paperwork did not have to be rebuilt to follow it. Identity is assigned at the desk, before anything is collected. Because the identifier was fixed before collection, the laboratory could change its testing strategy in a morning without rebuilding any paperwork. At four thousand a day we were close to what our instruments could do. That is the honest ceiling, and it is the answer to the obvious objection. Removing the copying did not raise the analytical capacity of the laboratory by a factor of thirteen. It let us reach the capacity we already had. Before, the machines were idle behind a queue of handwriting. Afterwards they ran near their limit. The bottleneck was the desk, not the bench. Analytical capacity was the same in both states. Removing the copying did not raise it. It let the laboratory reach it. The identifiers did something else that mattered more than speed. We could attach whatever fields we wanted to a record and check them against each other, so a wrong birth year or a swapped tube had several chances to be caught rather than none. Speed was the visible gain. Fewer misidentified samples was the one that mattered. I built it in a spreadsheet. Nobody procured anything. There was no vendor to wait for, so when the situation changed I changed it that same day, and there was no new budget line and no new staff. I want to be clear that this is not a story about my cleverness. It is a story about how low the barrier already was in 2021, and it is lower now. The same thing today could be assembled far faster than I assembled it. The principle has not changed at all. We did not hire any new staff. We had the exact same team of laboratory workers. We did not receive any new budget line to make this happen. The process was cheap, and it was entirely ours. It worked so well that the exact same process still runs at Vinh Long CDC today. It has survived because it fits the daily reality of a provincial laboratory. When I look back on those hard days, I see a clear truth. I realized that our problem was never really about speed. We did not need to run faster. We did not need to work ourselves to exhaustion. The real problem was the trace. The trace is the thread that connects a person to their sample. If you cannot guarantee that trace, speed is meaningless. It does not matter how many thousands of tests you run if you lose the connection between the person and the tube. The ID we created was not just a label. It was the physical anchor of that trace. It was the system that held our memory. During those years, I watched my colleagues walk away. They did not leave because they hated the science. They left because they could not afford to stay. In the provincial public health system, the hardest people to retain are always the preventive medicine staff. I lived this reality every single day, and the numbers in the literature match exactly what I felt on the laboratory floor. To understand why we lose these people, you have to look at how medical professionals make a living in Vietnam. A clinical doctor or nurse working in a hospital has an escape hatch. When their official shift ends, they can go to work at a private clinic. They can open their own practice or consult for private facilities. They have a source of private practice side income. But we do not have that option. A preventive medicine specialist cannot open a private clinic in the evening to track epidemics or test water quality. There is no private market for tracking diseases. Dieleman and colleagues documented this reality back in 2003. They found that the low salary and allowances at the commune and district levels were the main factors that destroyed motivation. Specifically, they noted that preventive medicine staff are the hardest to keep precisely because they lack the private practice income that clinical staff rely on ( 1 ) . The financial strain is not just a complaint. It is a documented barrier. In 2013, Tran and his co-authors studied health worker satisfaction at the commune level in Vietnam. Their findings were stark. Only 24.0 percent of the workers they surveyed were satisfied with their salary and allowances. Think about that number. Nearly three quarters of the staff were dissatisfied with their base pay. The dissatisfaction went deeper than just the monthly envelope. Only 25.1 percent of those workers felt satisfied with their overall benefits. When it came to the physical tools of the trade, only 35.7 percent were satisfied with the available equipment. Even the working environment itself only managed a 41.8 percent satisfaction rate ( 2 ) . I remember sitting in our administrative room, looking at my colleagues, and knowing these percentages were real. We worked with outdated machines and struggled to find basic supplies. Our base pay was low, and there were no evening consultations to make up the difference. When you live on those margins, every month is a quiet struggle. This is why we are writing this proposal. We cannot simply expect people to stay out of pure devotion. The data has shown for decades that the lack of private practice income and the dismal satisfaction with salary, benefits, and equipment are draining our provincial teams of their best talent. If we want to secure our health system, we must address the invisibility of this work and build a career path that keeps these specialists from walking out the door. What we lost was not equipment. It was people. After the extreme strain of 2021, we desperately hoped for a period of stability. Instead, we experienced a quiet, massive departure. What happened next was a crisis of retention that changed the landscape of public health across our entire country. According to the official Ministry of Health records, a staggering 9,680 public health staff left or quit their jobs between January 2021 and June 2022. This was not a minor shift. Among those who walked away from the public system, there were 3,094 doctors and 2,874 nurses. These departures were not evenly distributed throughout our provinces. Instead, they were heavily concentrated in our largest urban areas where the pressure had been highest. Ho Chi Minh City alone lost 2,035 health workers during this period. Hanoi, our capital, lost 1,032. Even in our provincial laboratories, the vacuum was completely real. When colleagues left, their empty desks meant more night shifts and more exhausting work for those of us who stayed behind ( 3 – 5 ) . The government recognized this severe crisis and tried to respond. They chose the most direct tool they had available. In early 2023, they issued Decree 05/2023. This decree raised the occupational allowance to 100 percent for preventive health and grassroots medical staff. For a brief moment, it felt like our struggle was finally recognized. Our monthly income went up, and we hoped this financial support would help stabilize our depleted workforce ( 6 ) . However, this intervention had a significant catch that destroyed its long-term impact. The 100 percent allowance was not a permanent wage reform. The decree only applied this increased rate temporarily for the period from January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2023. Starting on January 1, 2024, the occupational allowance reverted back to the old, much lower levels set by the earlier Decree 56/2011. Money was tried here as a solution, but it was tried temporarily, and it did not hold people ( 6 ) . This temporary measure proved exactly what many of us knew from our daily lives. Financial incentives alone are not enough to retain staff when they are applied in isolation. It was a brief bandage on a deep, structural problem. It did not create a predictable career pathway, nor did it make our daily field labor visible. When the temporary allowance expired in 2024, the extra financial support vanished, and the old sense of professional invisibility returned. My colleagues did not just want a short-term cash injection to endure burnout. They wanted a sustainable professional future where their verified work is recognized. This is why we need a new approach, because temporary money has already failed to keep our specialists from leaving ( 6 ) . Many colleagues pack their bags and leave. When people talk about solving this retention crisis, they almost always point to money. They demand larger bonuses, higher allowances, or direct pay-for-performance schemes. As someone who lived on a low public salary, I understand this demand. Money is not wrong. For underpaid staff in developing countries, salary is not merely a hygiene factor that we can ignore. It is a matter of basic survival. However, if we look closely at the global evidence on health worker retention, we find an honest and far more complicated picture. The scientific evidence on using financial incentives to retain health staff is surprisingly thin and inconsistent. Consider the 2021 Cochrane systematic review by Diaconu and colleagues. They analyzed pay-for-performance schemes in low and middle-income countries. They found that these financial programs produced inconsistent effects, and they graded the certainty of this evidence as low to very low. Even the World Health Organization is remarkably candid about the limitations of its own guidelines. In its official recommendations on retaining health workers in remote and rural areas, the WHO states that almost all of its retention recommendations rest on low or very low certainty evidence. This low grading is due to research design limitations, rather than proof that the interventions do not work. For instance, their recommendation on providing social recognition for rural health workers is graded as strong, yet the evidence backing it is rated as very low certainty ( 7 – 9 ) . We must look at how health workers make choices when they are asked directly. Discrete choice experiments allow us to see what staff value. In Timor-Leste, a study by Rockers and colleagues in 2016 surveyed over four hundred workers. They found that professional skills upgrading and specialization actually ranked above wages as the number one preference. In Lao PDR, a 2013 study by Miyazaki and colleagues found a slightly different mix. There, salary alongside secure tenure and promotion dominated the preferences of health workers. These studies suggest that career pathways often matter as much as, or even more than, direct cash. But we must attach a vital caveat to these findings. These are discrete choice experiments. They measure stated preferences on a survey, which does not always predict actual human behavior in real life ( 10 , 11 ) . We do not have randomized controlled trials comparing scholarships directly to cash rewards for frontline staff. What we do have is a clear pattern. Financial incentives alone are the weakest tool when applied in isolation. If we only try to throw temporary money at burnout, we will fail to build a sustainable public health service. We have to build a career pathway that makes our labor visible. The foundation of global policy rests on the World Health Organization’s 2010 global policy recommendations on retention in remote and rural areas and the 2021 guideline that replaced them. Both of these landmark documents are organized around four core pillars: education, regulation, financial incentives, and personal and professional support. Both guidelines explicitly state that coordinated, bundled packages of interventions always beat single, isolated interventions. More importantly, they agree that relying on financial incentives alone is the weakest standalone bet we can make. Yet, we must preserve the honest caveat that the World Health Organization itself attaches to these findings. The organization openly states that almost all of its own recommendations in this area rest on low or very low certainty evidence. This low certainty is a result of research design limitations in the field, not because these interventions have been proven ineffective. The Cochrane review conducted by Grobler and colleagues in 2015, registered as CD005314.pub3, evaluated the global literature and reached the exact same conclusion, finding very low certainty evidence for every single intervention type. title: Timekeeping or Scorekeeping
text: 2 Timekeeping or Scorekeeping The administrative office of our provincial CDC is quiet at five in the morning. On the desk, a printed list of names lies next to a keyboard. A stack of blank transport medium tubes sits in their plastic racks, clean and empty. Beside them, the barcode printer waits, its green status light blinking slow. I am wearing my ordinary clothes, a faded cotton shirt and trousers. There are no clinical samples in this room yet, so there is no need for a hazmat suit, heavy blue gown, or double layers of gloves. But as I look at the paper list under the fluorescent tube, a quiet realization comes over me. This desk work is the most dangerous step of the entire pandemic response. I open the email that arrived an hour ago. The messaging app on my phone is already buzzing with new lists sent by district teams. There are names of citizens quarantined in facilities after arriving from overseas, names of prisoners from the provincial jail, and names of people who died overnight in their homes. I begin transcribing them. My fingers move across the keys, converting the text into a structured Excel file. I connect the file to the barcode software and hit print. The machine hums, spitting out small, sticky labels with black-and-white lines. I peel each one and wrap it around a blank plastic tube. This barcode is a unique identifier, a digital thread that will bind this patient’s identity to their specimen from the moment of collection to the final diagnostic result. Outside this office, everyone associates our response with the drama of biological hazards. They think of the ambulance engine starting up, or whatever vehicle our unit could find to transport the teams. They think of the cold boxes, whether foam or ordinary ice boxes, being loaded for the run. They think of the wide corridor outside, where those cold boxes are currently being lined up. Yet, we cannot go out to collect a single sample until these labels are ready. If a barcode is printed with a wrong digit or stuck to the wrong tube, a patient’s result is lost, and the chain of containment breaks. We used to move fewer than three hundred samples a day, and the ceiling was this desk, not the bench. With identifiers fixed here before anything goes to the field, the same team can put four thousand through the day: the samples can be pooled into shared reactions and broken apart again when one comes back positive, without a single record being written out a second time. The instruments then run near their own limit, which is where the real ceiling sits. Same staff. No new budget line. This administrative routine is still running in our department today. I finish pasting the last label. The plastic tubes are now ready to be packed into the cold boxes. I look down at my hands, still free of gloves. The real bottleneck of the crisis is not happening in a secure laboratory or a quarantine ward. It is happening here, at a wooden desk, in everyday clothes, under the hum of an office light. In those five years, I did not just handle samples. I watched how people responded to the systems around them. During my time in the laboratory, I observed a fundamental truth about data. The exact same set of records can produce two completely opposite human reactions. It all depends on who owns that data. Under one frame, which we can call the timekeeping mindset, workers feel watched and monitored. They see the system as an intrusive eye. It is a tool of surveillance that tracks their minutes and counts their mistakes. When people feel controlled, they do not want to cooperate. They hide their efforts, they resist, and they do only the bare minimum required to avoid trouble. But there is another frame. If you shift the design so that workers are building their own records, the entire dynamic changes. Under this framework, the data belongs to them. It is their point-accumulation system, a physical ledger of their own sweat and labor. When workers know that they own the record of their own work, they do not hide. They actively step forward to volunteer the evidence of their achievements. They want to log every hour, every field visit, and every test because they are building a professional asset that belongs to them. This dramatic shift in behavior is not just an observation from our laboratory floor. It is explained by Self-Determination Theory, a psychological framework that highlights our basic needs for autonomy and competence. While researchers consider the core psychological mechanism of this theory to be strong, they rate its direct application in workplace systems as moderate. According to this theory, the way we frame a system changes everything. The theory draws a sharp distinction between informational rewards and controlling rewards. Informational rewards are those that confirm our competence and acknowledge our skills. When a worker receives feedback that confirms their mastery, their intrinsic motivation rises. They feel a sense of pride and professional growth. Controlling rewards, on the other hand, are designed to pressure, monitor, and push people. They are tools of control that signal to the worker that they are under constant surveillance. When a system relies on controlling rewards and pressure, motivation drops. This psychological reality tells us something vital about system design. The way we frame a system is not a minor cosmetic detail. It is a core design variable. How we structure the flow of data is what determines whether the system succeeds or fails. In my proposal, I am not asking for a more expensive system to watch our staff. I am proposing that we change the frame entirely. We need to stop using data to monitor people and start letting people use data to build themselves up. When we make this shift, we transform invisible field labor into a verified professional asset. This is the difference between a system of surveillance and a ladder of opportunity. I am writing this proposal because I know what it is like to work in the shadows, where your sweat has no physical record. Many people think that motivating health workers requires complex schemes or expensive campaigns. But as I sat at my desk and looked at the global literature on human behavior, I discovered the strongest evidence for our proposal. It shows that the simple act of tracking your own progress is a powerful force. This is not a vague claim. In 2016, Harkin and his colleagues published a landmark meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin. They compiled data from 138 independent studies, representing roughly 19,951 participants. Their findings were clear. They found that monitoring progress alone raised goal attainment. It did so with a substantial effect size of 0.40. But there was a vital detail in their findings that speaks directly to my experience in the laboratory. They discovered that this positive effect was even larger when progress was physically recorded. It was also larger when that recorded progress was reported or made public. This is the true pillar of our entire design. The value of this system does not lie in trivial gamified badges or superficial point systems. The value lies in the physical, verified recording of a worker’s daily labor. It is the act of turning invisible actions into a permanent record ( 1 – 3 ) . One limit belongs with that finding before I lean on it. Harkin and colleagues were synthesising studies of people pursuing their own goals: losing weight, giving up cigarettes, keeping to a course of study. Nobody in those trials was building a record that an employer, an auditor or a scholarship board would later read. Carrying the result across to a high-stakes workplace log is an extrapolation, and I am making it deliberately rather than quietly. The mechanism is plausible and the direction is probably right, but it has not been tested where the record decides something about the person keeping it. ( 3 ) We must look at how this physical record changes how a worker feels about their employer. In our field, people walk away because they feel completely invisible and unsupported. This feeling is captured by a concept called Perceived Organizational Support, or POS. In 2017, Kurtessis and his colleagues published a massive meta-analysis in the Journal of Management. They looked at how this sense of support correlates with employee behavior. The numbers they found are remarkably strong. A worker’s perceived organizational support has a massive positive correlation of 0.69 with their commitment to the organization. When staff feel supported, their intention to leave drops significantly, with a negative correlation of minus 0.50. Their actual rate of quitting drops as well, with a correlation of minus 0.21 ( 4 ) . But how do we build that sense of support in a provincial laboratory? The meta-analysis by Kurtessis and his team found that development opportunities are among the strongest sources of perceived organizational support. Giving people a chance to grow is far more powerful than temporary bonuses. This is why our proposal links a verified record of service to tangible educational gateways like scholarships. We are not just printing labels or tracking hours for surveillance. We are creating a physical record of competence that a worker can use to claim a professional future. When we do this, we transform the daily grind into a visible ladder of growth, backed by the strongest psychological science we have ( 4 ) . During those years of high stress, I often heard suggestions from visiting consultants about how to motivate our staff. They frequently proposed setting up leaderboards. They wanted us to display a public ranking of who processed the most sample tubes or who logged the most hours in the field. They believed that public competition would naturally drive us to work harder and faster. In my proposal, however, you will find no leaderboards. I have intentionally excluded them from the design of this recognition pathway. This decision is not a matter of personal taste. It is guided by what actually happens when you introduce ranking systems to frontline health workers. We should look at the real-world evidence from field research. A recent study on the design of gamified training systems for community health workers found something very clear. Frontline workers do not read public ranking systems as a source of healthy motivation. Instead, they read them as tools of surveillance. When you introduce public scores, it creates a high level of anxiety. It breeds resistance and tension inside a professional environment where people must rely on one another to survive. In our laboratories and field units, we do not work in isolation. We work in tight, interdependent teams. Furthermore, the broader literature on gamification supports this caution. A systematic review by Sailer and Homner in 2020 analyzed the actual effectiveness of these game-like elements. They found that pure competition alone consistently underperforms when compared to competition combined with collaboration. When you force people to compete against their colleagues without any cooperative element, the team dynamics break down. Even more importantly, their meta-analysis showed that when you look at high-rigor studies, most of the grand claims about gamification begin to fade. They looked at cognitive, motivational, and behavioral effects. Only the cognitive effect of gamification actually held up under high-rigour analysis. The behavioral and emotional changes that marketers promise simply do not survive strict scientific scrutiny ( 5 ) . We must be honest about what we do not know. There is currently no randomized controlled trial evaluating the use of points, badges, or leaderboards for community health worker performance in low and middle-income countries. The trials simply do not exist. What has been documented to work in these settings is financial incentives tied directly to verified activities. Public rankings, on the other hand, are what consistently backfire. For these reasons, the pathway I am proposing relies on self-competition. People should compete only against their own past record, not against their colleagues. A worker’s dashboard will show their own progress, their own verified hours, and their own path toward their educational goals. It will not show where they stand in a public hierarchy. We want to build a tool that confirms competence and records sweat, not a scoreboard that publicizes shame. When we remove the leaderboard, we remove the feeling of being watched, and we allow workers to focus on their own growth. During those years, I filled out my share of paperwork. We would often sit down at the end of the month, try to remember what we had done weeks earlier, and write it down on paper sheets. But as I write this proposal, I must be completely honest about this practice. A paper log submitted at the end of the month is not actual scientific evidence of work. It is a statement. It is a retrospective claim, a recollection of events that is highly prone to human error and fading memory. Real data integrity requires something much more rigorous. The global pharmaceutical and medical industries have already named the standard we must follow. It is called ALCOA. This standard was originally coined by Stan Woollen at the United States Food and Drug Administration in the early 1990s. He created it as a simple mnemonic device to train inspectors. Over time, through widespread adoption across clinical trials and manufacturing, this mnemonic became the global gold standard for data integrity ( 6 ) . It is important to note a vital caveat here. These standards were written for regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing and clinical laboratories. None of them were originally designed for a provincial preventive medicine lab in Vietnam. Applying them in our provincial CDC is a deliberate borrowing of an industry standard, not a legal requirement. Yet, if we want our records to be trusted internationally, this is the bar we must meet. The very first letter in this standard stands for Attributable. To be attributable, a record must show exactly who performed an action and when they did it. This information must be tied directly to a unique individual identity. In many provincial laboratories, staff often share a single computer login or sign off on sheets using a generic team name. This is a classic inspection finding because shared logins completely break accountability. If everyone is logged in as the same user, the trace is gone. You cannot verify who actually ran a test or who made a change. The third letter in the standard stands for Contemporaneous. This means recording the data at the exact moment the work is performed. Writing logs late, keeping rough notes on scraps of paper to copy them later, or batching data entry at the end of the day is not a minor paperwork error. In the eyes of international inspectors, it is a direct violation of data integrity. This is why we need to build a digital pathway that records work as it happens. When a technician scans a barcode on a container tube, the database must log that action instantly with their unique identity. We cannot rely on retrospective paper statements compiled weeks after the fact. I have to secure a contemporaneous, attributable record. That is the only way to transform our invisible daily sweat into a verified professional asset that outside institutions can trust. During that time, I saw how easily human memory fails when it is forced to do paperwork weeks after the fact. In this proposal, I want to address the second core letter of the ALCOA standard: Contemporaneous. In the world of high-standard data integrity, contemporaneous means that an activity must be recorded at the exact moment it happens. It cannot wait. When recording happens hours or weeks after the work, certain practices appear everywhere, and they appear for the same reason. Logs get completed after the fact. Numbers get written on whatever paper is at hand and transcribed into the official ledger later. Entry gets batched to the end of a long day. None of this comes from dishonesty. It comes from a system that was designed to make people remember instead of designed to let them record. Under international data standards these practices are treated as data integrity failures, and the standards are right about the consequence: the record stops being trustworthy. But the fix does not belong to the person holding the pen. It belongs to whoever designed the moment at which the pen is picked up. To prevent these failures, we must design a system that complies with the highest regulatory rules, like the United States Food and Drug Administration’s 21 CFR Part 11. Specifically, section 11.10(e) requires a computer-generated, time-stamped audit trail that records every creation, modification, or deletion. The rule states that any change must not obscure previously recorded information. Compliant laboratory systems do meet that rule, with append-only audit tables, database controls and digital signatures. What they generally do not add is cryptographic immutability that holds against the system’s own administrator, and no rule requires them to. The audit trail answers to the institution that runs it. This means that if we build a system where a record is pushed immediately to a server and secured unalterably using cryptography, we are actually performing above the current regulatory standard rather than merely catching up to it. There is a limit to what this technology can do, and it is worth naming before anyone gets excited about cryptography. A tamper-proof log of fabricated entries is still a tamper-proof lie. Cryptography cannot prevent a technician from lying about a test they never ran. Because of this limitation, the whole idea of our digital design is mistake-proofing. In manufacturing, they call this poka-yoke. We should not waste our time telling stressed, overworked frontline staff not to do things wrong. We should not rely on constant warnings or heavy training manuals. Instead, we should build a workflow where the easy path is the correct one. When a technician scans a barcode, the time and the identity are fixed at that moment, so writing the entry up from memory a week later stops being the convenient option. I want to be exact about the limit here, because it matters. A scan proves that a label was read at a particular second. It does not prove that a specimen was drawn, and nothing stops somebody scanning fifty tubes at a desk. Contemporaneous capture removes the drift that comes from writing things down later. It is not a defence against someone who has decided to lie, and the later layers exist because of that. By securing the data at the moment of creation, we make integrity the only path forward. During that time, I learned that you cannot build a sustainable health system on guesswork. When we design tools to motivate frontline workers, we must rely on honest, proven mechanics from behavioral research rather than marketing hype. Our proposal does not try to invent human behavior. Instead, we want to look at how people actually respond to progress and thresholds, using established science while remaining completely honest about its limits. The first behavioral concept we must build upon is the endowed progress effect. In 2006, researchers Nunes and Drèze published a field experiment studying how people complete tasks. They compared two scenarios. In the first, people received a loyalty card with eight blank spaces. In the second, they received a ten-space card that already had two pre-stamped marks. Technically, both groups needed to complete exactly eight tasks to reach the goal. Yet, the group with the pre-stamped cards showed a much higher completion rate, rising from 19 percent to 34 percent. The feeling of already being on a journey is a powerful psychological driver. title: Three Readers, One Record
text: 3 Three Readers, One Record At three o’clock on a rainy Tuesday afternoon, three people are looking at the exact same line of data on their screens. In our provincial laboratory in Vietnam, a technician named Vy stares at a row of text showing forty-eight polymerase chain reaction cycles completed at midnight. For her, this line is her only shield, the physical proof of her ten-hour night shift. Down the hall, her supervisor looks at the same line because a query about a contaminated batch just arrived. For him, this row of text is a liability map, a way to find who is answerable for the error. Thousands of miles away in an air-conditioned office, a program officer opens a database. He has never seen our cramped room, but he paid for the reagents. For him, this line is a consumption metric, proof that the materials did not expire in a warehouse. All three are reading the same entry at the same moment. Yet, they see three entirely different realities. Our data served the institution, the funder and the auditor. It did not serve the person who produced it, and nobody designed it that way on purpose. Modern laboratory informatics has built sophisticated tracking systems that view attribution purely as an instrument of blame and auditing. In Vietnam, thirty-eight laboratories have implemented open-source LIMS with US CDC support. However, these systems are managed provincially and lack individual, machine-enforced audit trails. When something goes wrong, we search the logs to find who to punish. When something goes right, the technician’s labor remains completely invisible. Our proposal is to turn this shared line of data into a voluntary point-accumulation asset owned by the worker. Rather than using it as a top-down surveillance tool, the technician can export her own verified contributions as a portable professional credential. This shift from surveillance to self-owned progress is supported by strong behavioral science. Meta-analyses on Perceived Organizational Support show that development opportunities are among the strongest drivers of employee commitment. It is necessary to design this registry carefully to avoid the traps of gamification. For instance, studies on status tiers show that demoting an individual damages loyalty, so our system will never demote a user. We also reject daily streaks and point expiration, which behavioral literature shows can lead to data gaming or burnout. Instead, we rely on established concepts like endowed progress, where providing an initial, justified jumpstart on a progress record has been shown to increase completion rates from nineteen to thirty-four percent in field experiments. However, we must remain completely honest about our limits. While behavioral mechanisms like endowed progress and goal gradients are well-documented in marketing studies, their application to healthcare is mostly untested. There is currently absolutely no trial evidence or randomized controlled studies evaluating how a worker-owned, point-accumulation registry affects reporting accuracy or staff retention in low-resource public health laboratories. We are proposing a logical, evidence-informed pilot of twelve months to test these ideas. By connecting the machine’s serial number to a technician’s name, we can satisfy the supervisor’s need for accountability, the funder’s need for tracking, and the worker’s need for visible, portable credit. Many digital systems and data initiatives come and go. Most of them arrived with a great deal of noise, only to end up abandoned. They died because of a fundamental flaw in their architecture. They were built for only one party. In the world of public health, if you design a system that serves only a single group, you are writing its death sentence. Most of the tools we were forced to use were built entirely for the funder. The international donors or the high-level administrators wanted clean reports and compliance metrics. Because the system was designed only for their eyes, we on the laboratory floor felt policed and monitored. We saw the software as an intrusive eye that tracked our minutes without offering us any value. When staff feel watched, they naturally resist. They find ways to work around the system, or worse, they begin to fabricate numbers just to make the charts look green. The data becomes a performance, and the system dies of its own falsehood. Conversely, you can try to build a system solely for the worker. You can design an app that helps us track our daily tasks or manage our own professional learning. But if the system serves only the worker, it hits a different wall. Nobody wants to pay to run it. Government agencies and international donors will not fund a platform that does not provide them with verified, actionable data. Without their financial support, the technology cannot survive, and the project quickly collapses once the initial enthusiasm fades. The proposal does not choose between those readers. It rests on one observation: the same record can serve all three of them at once. For the worker, the record is a self-owned portfolio of verified labor. It is their personal point-accumulation ledger that they can carry with them to unlock professional opportunities, like scholarships. For the funder, this very same record is trusted, tamper-evident proof of activity. They can see that the tests were actually run, satisfying their need for accountability without forcing us to feel policed. For the third reader, the educational partner or licensing body, the record is a credible proof of competence. They can instantly verify that a worker has met the required clinical standards without waiting weeks for manual verification. One record, three readers. The same row of data, read by three parties who currently want different things from it. Nothing new is collected; only who may read it changes. We should be entirely honest about the limits of this design. A tamper-proof log of fabricated entries is still just a tamper-proof lie. Technology alone cannot prevent a technician from entering false data at the start. However, by aligning the interests of all three readers into one shared record, we remove the main incentive to cheat. We transform a tool of surveillance into a mutual asset. Our staff struggle under a system that made their daily labor completely invisible. When we write logs or enter data, we are creating records that could serve multiple purposes. Yet, most systems fail because they are built to be read by only one party. In this proposal, I want to describe a system that is designed for two distinct readers at the same time, using the exact same digital record. The first reader of this record is the worker. Today, if a technician spends five years running thousands of PCR tests in a provincial lab, they leave with nothing but a blank paper resume. They have no portable proof of their work. I am proposing a self-owned digital portfolio that is a permanent, verified record of their actual labour. It is a record that says, for example, I performed four thousand two hundred verified diagnostic tests over these specific years under a unique digital signature. This is not a symbolic badge or a superficial points system. It is a portable professional asset. It belongs entirely to the worker, and they can carry it with them when they move between different employers or apply for advanced training. The second reader of this record is the institution. In our current provincial labs, there is often deep confusion about who did what on any given day. To solve this, our proposal borrows the strict data integrity standards of the international pharmaceutical industry, specifically the ALCOA framework. In these standards, the very first letter stands for Attributable. This means a record must show exactly who performed a test and when they did it, mapped against a unique digital identity. When an institution reads our proposed database, they gain absolute clarity about individual responsibility. They can see exactly who processed each tube, who ran each assay, and who verified the results. However, we must be completely honest about the limits of this design and preserve some important caveats. The ALCOA standard was originally created for highly regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing and clinical trial laboratories. None of these regulations were written for a provincial preventive medicine laboratory in Vietnam. Applying them here is a deliberate borrowing of high-status industry practices, not a legal requirement. Furthermore, in the existing industry frameworks, attribution is treated almost entirely as a mechanism of blame and auditing. It is designed to find out who to blame when a record is wrong or when a test fails. Shared logins are a classic inspection finding because they destroy this accountability. The breakthrough of our design is that we do not use attribution to police or blame our staff. Instead, we transform this institutional record of responsibility into a positive, portable professional credit owned by the worker. We make the same record serve both the technician and the institution without adding administrative weight. In those years, I handled thousands of diagnostic test kits bought with international donor money. I saw how much effort went into tracking these resources. Yet, as I write this proposal, I must point out a massive gap in how we account for these materials. This brings us to the third reader of our proposed record: the funder. Under our design, the donor finally gains the ability to see exactly when a reagent bought with its money was used, by whom it was used, and for what specific test. To understand why this is a breakthrough, we must look at how donor commodities are tracked today. The global health system relies on major supply chain programmes and software platforms like OpenLMIS. These systems are supported by organizations like Gavi and the Global Fund. But if you look closely at these tools, they only trace commodities as far as the physical facility. They show that a box of reagents arrived at a provincial warehouse or was delivered to a specific clinic. After that, the trace goes completely cold. The systems can only record aggregate consumption. They cannot link a specific vial of chemical reagent to an individual diagnostic test. They cannot tell you which named operator actually ran the test, or on which day, or for which patient. ( 1 , 2 ) Some people argue that modern instrument connectivity solves this problem. Many laboratories use middleware to connect high-throughput machines, such as viral load analyzers, directly to database systems. But this connectivity does not solve the human accountability gap. It attributes activity to a physical machine rather than a named person. The system logs that the analyzer ran fifty tests, but it does not tell you who prepared the samples, who calibrated the instrument, or who was responsible for the run. Where the trace goes cold. Current tracking terminates at the clinic door and the machine casing. The proposal extends the same trace by one more step, to the person who ran the test. It is worth being exact about what exists today and what does not. There is currently no open-source laboratory information management system in low and middle-income countries that features cryptographic immutability by default. No international donor currently requires tracing chemical reagents down to individual operators. Implementing this level of traceability is our own deliberate design choice, not a legal mandate or a donor requirement. Furthermore, we must state a hard truth. A tamper-proof log of fabricated entries is still just a tamper-proof lie. If a laboratory technician enters false data at the start, cryptography cannot prevent that dishonesty. We must still rely on spot-audits and supervisor co-signatures to verify the input. By closing this gap, we transform how donors view their investments. Instead of just seeing shipments arrive at a building, they see their funding actively turn into verified human labor on the laboratory floor. Much hard work goes completely unrecorded. In this proposal, I want to address the most significant gap in our entire global health data architecture. When you look at how laboratory data is managed today, every single existing framework treats attribution as a mechanism for blame and auditing. In these regulatory structures, knowing who performed an action is only useful when something goes wrong. If a data entry is incorrect, or if an assay fails, the system is used to identify the person responsible. It is a tool for policing and finding fault. Shared logins are treated as major inspection findings because they break this chain of blame. Yet, this focus on fault-finding wastes something. Currently, no regulator, no laboratory information system, no logistics platform, and no international donor has turned this very same record into positive, portable credit owned by the person who performed the work. If a technician runs four thousand tests over three years with absolute precision, that achievement is completely lost to history. The system logs their name for auditing, but they leave their job with a blank paper resume. There is absolutely no established standard for exporting a verified service history as a professional asset. Under the current system, a worker’s hard labor is treated as an institutional commodity rather than their own professional property. We have built elaborate, expensive structures to trace reagents and monitor machinery, but we have completely failed to build a mechanism that allows workers to own the proof of their own competence. It is worth being plain about the existing tools and their limitations. Some administrative platforms, such as iHRIS or the Workload Indicators of Staffing Need tool, are designed to track staffing numbers, training levels, and overall workload estimates. However, these systems remain completely disconnected from actual daily laboratory logs. Other modern security frameworks, such as blockchain protocols for auditing electronic health records, are designed to log who accessed or edited files. Yet, their focus is entirely on data security and detecting abuse. They were never intended to record positive professional achievements or provide portable career credits. Furthermore, we must acknowledge a vital caveat. No open-source laboratory database in low and middle-income countries currently features cryptographic immutability by default, and no international donor requires tracing work down to individual operators. Implementing this in our local clinics is a choice, not a legal requirement. By transforming the institutional audit trail into a verified service record, we can allow workers to own their professional history. This turns a tool of surveillance into a ladder of opportunity, helping the unconnected prove their worth. When we talk about global health, we often speak in terms of charity or moral obligation. But in this proposal, There is a version of this argument addressed to funders, and I will put it plainly rather than at length. Programmes that support laboratory capacity abroad do so on the reasoning that detection is cheaper and earlier at the source. That reasoning depends on the people at the source still being there next year. This is the honest reading of what our proposed system is and what it is not. I must state a vital caveat from the outset. This recognition pathway is not an early warning system itself. It will not automatically detect a new pathogen or trigger an emergency alert. Instead, it is the quiet machinery that keeps the workforce operating the early warning system from falling apart. By transforming invisible daily sweat into a verified professional asset, we ensure that trained technicians stay in their jobs longer and produce more timely, reliable diagnostic data. We are securing the human foundation of health security. Without stable, motivated people on the laboratory floor, even the most expensive surveillance machinery is useless. The cost of failing to stop health threats at their source is staggering. To understand the scale of this risk, we can look at the economic impact of the last major global crisis. According to a 2020 paper by Cutler and Summers published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, COVID-19 cost the United States roughly 16 trillion dollars. This is an almost unimaginable sum of money. However, we must preserve the strict honesty caveats attached to this figure. First, the text notes that about half of that 16 trillion dollar estimate represents non-market health loss, such as the value of lost lives and mental health impacts, rather than direct lost economic output. Second, we must acknowledge that this paper is a short viewpoint article rather than a peer-reviewed, complex economic modeling study. It is a simplified estimate, not a definitive final calculation ( 3 , 4 ) . Yet, even with these necessary caveats, the message is undeniable. The economic and human cost of a delayed response dwarfs any local investment in public health systems. When a provincial laboratory in a place like Vietnam cannot retain its staff, the delay in detecting a novel threat can ripple across oceans in days. By investing in a digital pathway that verifies and honors the work of frontline technicians, the United States keeps the people who operate that capacity in place. Equipment is the part that gets counted. The person who runs it at two in the morning is the part that walks away, and replacing her costs more than keeping her. During that time, I watched valuable investments quietly decay. When we talk about global health security, we often look at the staggering scale of the financial numbers involved. If we look at the cost of global pandemic preparedness, the figures presented by major international health bodies are massive. The G20 High Level Independent Panel, in its July 2021 report, estimated that global pandemic preparedness requires roughly 15 billion dollars a year in additional international funding. Just a few months later, in March 2022, the World Health Organization and the World Bank presented a report to the G20 estimating the total preparedness need at 31.1 billion dollars a year, with 10.5 billion of that representing additional international funding. On these numbers, the record deserves a plain statement. They are not bottom-up cost calculations with precise confidence intervals. Instead, they are expert consensus estimates designed primarily for policy advocacy ( 3 – 5 ) . Some advocates attempt to justify these massive investments by quoting dramatic return-on-investment multiples, but these two numbers differ by orders of magnitude. In this proposal, I deliberately refuse to quote any specific return multiple. I do this because those multiples are simple ratios rather than counterfactual models. They do not survive strict economic scrutiny and fail to account for complex real-world variables. However, the core of my argument does not rely on these grand global estimates. There is a deep cost asymmetry at play here. While the world debates tens of billions of dollars, the local reality on the laboratory floor is far more modest. This proposal does not ask for a single dollar of new, unallocated money. It does not ask for a new budget line from any donor or ministry. Instead, the real argument is that this proposal asks that what has already been invested does not decay ( 3 , 4 ) . In Vietnam, the marginal dollar should not be used to build new facilities or buy more high-throughput machinery. We already have a preventive health network that reaches all sixty-three provinces and extends down to the commune level. title: From Record to Door
text: 4 From Record to Door In London a surgical trainee opens his intercollegiate e-logbook and enters a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. His supervisor countersigns it the same day. Three years of hernia repairs, appendix removals and assisted incisions sit in that file, each one dated, each one signed by somebody other than him. At national selection the panel does not ask him to describe his experience. It reads the count. At the same hour in a provincial CDC in Vietnam, a laboratory technician finishes her ten-thousandth polymerase chain reaction assay. She has been at the bench since the previous evening. When she logs off, the count goes nowhere. There is no file with her name on it, no countersignature, nothing a committee could read. Her five years exist in shift rosters and internal reports that were never built to leave the building, and in the memory of a supervisor who will retire. Two people, the same trade in the sense that both are trusted with a patient’s diagnosis, the same hour of the same day. One of them has a record. That is the whole of the difference, and it is not a difference in skill. During those long shifts of processing diagnostic assays, I watched how the absolute invisibility of our field work limits our professional lives. When we propose a digital registry to record the verified contributions of our technicians, we must look at the real-world models that actually work. The British surgical logbook, the flight logs of the Federal Aviation Administration, and the portfolios of the National Board for Professional Teaching Standards in the United States all share the same structural engine. They succeed because they meet three rigid conditions. First, the record is verified by an external supervisor. Second, the record is tied directly to a real career gateway held by an authority. Third, the reward is substantial, such as a specialized training slot or a salary upgrade, rather than a symbolic badge. The weakest link is worth naming first. Our technology can easily handle the verification of these records. However, the system only works if we can secure a real educational partner to hold open the career gateways. We are proposing tiered scholarships of twenty-five, fifty, and seventy-five percent for our certified technicians rather than symbolic micro-credentials, which have absolutely no independent evidence of improving promotion or retention in the scientific literature. Our daily work vanish into thin air. We ran thousands of critical assays, but when we went home, we had nothing to show for it. In this proposal, I am suggesting that we build a verified portfolio of labor. To some, this might sound like a theoretical experiment, but we do not need to invent this concept from scratch. We can look directly at three concrete, highly successful models that already run on this exact architecture. The first model is from the United Kingdom’s medical system. Surgical trainees do not rely on vague recommendations. Instead, they must maintain the Intercollegiate Surgical eLogbook and the ISCP portfolio. To even apply for advanced national selection for training, a surgeon must submit a verified logbook of their actual surgeries. These recorded case numbers are not symbolic. They directly feed official progress assessments like the ARCP and the final certification of completion of training. The second model is found in aviation. After the Colgan Air crash in 2009, Congress directed the Federal Aviation Administration to raise the experience required of airline pilots. The rule that resulted, 14 CFR 61.159, sets an airline transport pilot certificate at fifteen hundred hours of logged flight time, and 14 CFR 121.436 is what obliges the airline to hire only pilots who hold it. A logbook is not a resume builder in that system. It is the legal gate. ( 1 ) What matters more for this proposal is the part of the rule that is usually left out of the summary. The fifteen hundred hours are not absolute. A pilot who graduated from an approved four-year aviation degree can hold a restricted certificate at one thousand hours; a two-year degree brings it to twelve hundred and fifty; a military pilot to seven hundred and fifty. The regulator did not lower its standard for those pilots. It accepted a different, verified record in place of raw hours. That is exactly the shape of what I am proposing, and it already exists in American federal law, in a safety system with no appetite for sentiment. A verified record of structured work can substitute for a cruder count, provided somebody outside the applicant certifies it. ( 1 – 3 ) The third model belongs to education. In the United States, teachers can seek National Board Certification. To do this, they do not take a simple exam. They build a comprehensive portfolio consisting of classroom video recordings, actual student work, and deep written analysis. If their portfolio passes the national standards, it converts directly into a substantial annual stipend of five thousand to seven thousand dollars. These three diverse fields prove that a self-recorded log can become a powerful professional asset, but they also teach us that such systems only survive under three strict conditions. First, the records must be verified by an external party, such as a supervisor or an independent regulator. Second, the log must be tied to a real gate held by a real gatekeeper, like a license, a salary tier, or a training slot. Third, the reward must be substantial, like professional advancement or money, rather than symbolic digital badges. The weakest link in this proposal is the gate. A verified ledger of laboratory work is completely useless unless we have a real educational partner holding the door to actual scholarships. If we do not secure a partner to honor these records, we are handing our staff symbolic digital badges. Currently, there is absolutely no independent evidence proving that digital badges alone lead to promotions or pay rises. I have to secure a real gatekeeper to make this work. The first condition is that the record of labor must be verified by someone outside of the worker. A self-declared logbook holds no weight on its own. In a laboratory setting, a technician cannot simply write down that they ran a test and expect others to believe it. There must be an independent verifier, such as a laboratory supervisor, who confirms the entry using a unique digital signature. Without this external verification, the database is nothing more than a list of unproven claims. The second condition is that the log must be tied to a real door that someone already controls. In the UK surgical model, that door is a national selection panel for training. In American aviation, it is the legal gate to an airline first officer seat. For teachers in the United States, a complex portfolio of classroom video and student work converts directly into a substantial annual stipend. If we build a system of records without a corresponding gatekeeper who holds the keys to real career advancement, we are wasting our time. The record must lead directly to a specific, tangible opportunity that already exists in the administrative framework. The third condition is that the reward must be substantive. By substantive, we mean actual training opportunities, professional licensing, or direct financial compensation, such as an annual stipend. I have to not offer our workers symbolic tokens or digital badges. The honest position on this point and face a hard scientific caveat is this. There is currently no independent, peer-reviewed evidence proving that digital badges or micro-credentials alone convert into career promotion or salary increases. Every single claim of their effectiveness traces back to the marketing materials of the platforms that sell and issue these badges. There is no trial data supporting their value on their own. Our proposal is built on these three pillars. It is an honest design that avoids the trap of empty gamification. We do not want to give our underpaid frontline staff meaningless digital stickers. Instead, we want to build a verified record that connects directly to the existing legal rails of continuous medical education and real training slots. By respecting these three strict conditions, we can turn a simple laboratory log into a genuine professional asset that our workers can carry with them to build their futures. I know how easy it is to make a paper log look perfect. But when we talk about creating digital, immutable records of laboratory labor, we have to face a hard truth. A tamper-proof log of fabricated entries is still only a tamper-proof lie. Cryptography can prevent anyone from changing a record after it is saved, but it cannot stop a technician from entering fake data at the start. To solve this hardest of problems, we must build an objective verification layer. That layer is external quality assessment, commonly known as EQA. Under EQA, the laboratory is sent blind proficiency panels without any warning. Because these samples arrive randomly and are prepared by an external party, they cannot be self-reported, anticipated, or gamed. The technician must process them exactly like regular samples. EQA is not a speculative or experimental concept. It is globally recognized as the gold standard for laboratory quality. Participation in EQA is strictly mandatory under international standards like ISO 15189, which requires labs to join inter-laboratory comparison programs and document corrective actions when results drift. In the United States, passing proficiency testing under the CLIA rules is a mandatory condition of laboratory certification ( 4 – 6 ) . Vietnam is not starting from scratch here. We have a solid legal framework for this. Under Decision 2429 of 2017, issued by the Ministry of Health, laboratories are evaluated using a national quality criteria set. Our designated national quality control centres manage these schemes and publish national proficiency testing data. Furthermore, we have shown that we can push this high level of quality control deep into the field. The National Institute of Hygiene and Epidemiology and the Pasteur Institute have successfully taken external quality assessment down to the commune level for HIV testing. We have proven that even remote, rural health staff can participate in rigorous quality control networks ( 5 , 7 , 8 ) . However, we must be completely honest about the limits of these existing programs. Every EQA scheme running today is designed to assess the laboratory as a whole institution, not the individual worker. Currently, there is absolutely no published data on individual-level EQA performance for provincial CDC technicians in Vietnam. Suggesting that we already evaluate individual personnel through EQA here would be mere speculation. Furthermore, there is a real risk of purpose drift. Historically, under CLIA, laboratories have been caught giving special treatment to proficiency samples because the stakes were too high. When you turn EQA into a high-stakes test of an individual, you create a blame culture that forces people to hide errors rather than report them. To avoid this trap, our proposal does not record whether an individual passed or failed a panel. Instead, we log that a technician has successfully participated in a set number of external quality rounds under a rotation mechanism, alongside their documented corrective actions when discrepancies occurred. This proves true professional discipline without turning quality assessment into a game of fear. No system in the world has yet turned EQA participation into a portable individual credential, but by doing so, we can finally verify the worker’s true competence. Our staff struggle to prove their daily labor. In this proposal, I want to address a critical design correction regarding how we verify laboratory labor through external quality assessment, or EQA. Standard practice in global health always scores the laboratory as a whole institution, not the individual person. If you look at standard laboratory audits, this institutional focus seems absolute. However, there are some narrow, existing precedents for individual tracking that we must examine. Under the American CLIA rules, proficiency testing samples must be handled by the routine staff who actually perform the testing, and these samples must be rotated among them. This rotation means the specific individual running the sample is already documented in the laboratory’s records, and this proficiency testing can serve as a valid input for annual personnel competency assessments. Furthermore, the British NHS cervical screening programme goes even further and actively assesses individual staff competence, covering around one thousand one hundred and nineteen personnel across sixty-three laboratories twice a year, while schemes like UK NEQAS Digital Morphology also accept individual registrations. Therefore, our proposed system makes a vital design correction. The digital ledger will never show a personal pass or fail score for an individual technician. Instead, the database will document two things only. It will show a technician’s active participation across official sample rotations. It will also record their documented corrective action when a result was out of consensus with the reference group. Logging how a technician handles a discrepancy shows true professional discipline and honesty. It proves they can participate in a rigorous quality loop without turning quality assessment into a high-stakes test of fear. This design correction ensures that we protect data integrity while respecting the human limits of our frontline workforce. However, we must examine what the leading standards authorities say about using external quality assessment as a direct measure of an individual’s skill. The United Kingdom Accreditation Service, or UKAS, released a position paper in 2017 stating clearly that external quality assessment is not a compulsory component of assessing individual competence. Instead, EQA is designed to guarantee the overall quality of the service being delivered, not to act as a personal test. In agreement with this view, the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, or CLSI, frames competence as a multi-element assessment. In their QMS03 guideline, they explain that true competency evaluation must combine direct observation, result reviews, blind specimens, and problem-solving exercises. Relying on a single test score is inadequate. ( 9 , 10 ) The core of the trap lies in how we evaluate accuracy. When a monitoring system scores performance based on peer consensus, and the entire peer group begins to drift in the same direction, the accurate laboratory is suddenly the one that looks wrong. In this scenario, the person who reports truthfully becomes the outlier. Instead of being recognized for their precision, they are treated as an error that must be corrected. This is not a theoretical suspicion. Vietnam’s own published proficiency testing data across fifty-nine laboratories, published by Van and colleagues in 2023, shows a clear divergence. In their study of nine biochemical analytes across twelve samples, the expert group consensus actually diverged from the overall participant consensus on common analytes. This means that peer group divergence is a measured, documented phenomenon and not just a vague suspicion. It proves that peer groups can and do drift, and that the crowd is not always right. ( 9 , 11 ) If we build a registry that punishes the outlier, we will receive uniform reports, but we will not receive true ones. Technicians are rational actors. If telling the truth exposes them to administrative correction or shame, they will simply adjust their numbers to match the consensus. This defeats the entire purpose of public health surveillance. To avoid this, our proposed registry implements two critical design consequences. First, the record must be designed as an asset owned by the worker rather than an audit instrument held by the institution. Under a worker-owned model, honest recording builds your own professional capital and establishes your personal credibility. Under an institutional audit model, honest recording merely exposes you to punishment. Second, we must ensure that scoring references an objective laboratory method rather than a fluctuating crowd wherever it is possible. This anchors our evaluations in science rather than peer consensus. During those years of processing diagnostic samples under constant pressure, I dreamed of a way to make our labor visible. But as I write this proposal, I must state a vital, hard boundary before anyone else points it out. It is worth being plain about what our proposed verified service record cannot do. A verified digital work history, no matter how securely recorded on a digital ledger, cannot substitute for formal professional licensure or national board certification. The first gate is professional certification. The American Society for Clinical Pathology Board of Certification offers both a domestic route and an international route, known as ASCPi. For a foreign-trained technician, eligibility for the international medical laboratory scientist certification rests on a formal degree plus an accredited training program, or on a clinical degree plus three years of acceptable laboratory experience. If their degree is in biology or chemistry rather than laboratory science, the requirement rises to five years of clinical experience. Furthermore, before an applicant can even sit for the exam, their academic transcripts must pass through a strict credential evaluation service like WES or ECE. We must preserve the honest caveat that many employers do not treat the international ASCPi credential as equivalent to the domestic ASCP certification. The second gate is state licensing. About eleven states in the United States, including California and New York, license laboratory personnel separately from national certification. These states conduct their own audits, reviewing academic coursework hour by hour against their own rigid category lists. Because foreign transcripts are structured differently, they often fall short in a single chemistry or biology category. When this happens, the licensing board does not care about years of experience. The only accepted remedy is to go back to school and complete the missing coursework. The third gate is the visa, which is completely independent and is almost always the hardest barrier to cross. The honest conclusion is that our proposed digital record changes none of these rigid international rules. It does not waive a single coursework hour or bypass a visa interview. However, it does something that is worth far more than it first sounds. It makes the clinical experience route provable. To qualify for certification through experience, the board requires detailed proof of acceptable work in an accredited laboratory, verified directly by a laboratory director. Today, a technician from a provincial CDC in Vietnam has no credible way to prove their years of invisible labor to an international board. By providing a tamper-proof, verified history of their actual diagnostic contributions, we turn their silent service into a verifiable asset. It does not guarantee a visa, but it gives a hardworking technician a real fighting chance. We need to not make false promises to our workforce. This proposal does not offer a magic key to escape across borders. Instead, we must present this system for what it actually is, a tool to make the “N years of experience” route provable. It is a verified asset for postgraduate admissions, fellowship applications, and research roles where formal licenses are not required. By acknowledging these institutional barriers plainly, we protect our integrity and build a system that remains useful within its true boundaries.
